Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors: Soreness, cracking and dryness of skin on the palms for 3–4 months; intermittent itch; has bled when scratched; symptoms worse enough to miss 3 days of work; onset after job change to hotel housekeeping with frequent exposure to bathroom cleaning products and inconsistent glove use; prior trial of E45 emollient and an oral antihistamine without improvement; past medical history notable for type 2 diabetes.  
- Relevant family medical history: Family history of diabetes; no known family skin disease reported.  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications): Metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented; E45 emollient — OTC trial, dose/route/frequency not documented; Antihistamine — name/dose/route/frequency not documented.

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Key findings/impression from transcript: Middle-aged woman with 3–4 months of painful, fissured, itchy palmar dermatitis temporally related to starting hotel housekeeping work with frequent exposure to cleaning products and inconsistent glove use; type 2 diabetes noted and may predispose to skin problems; prior OTC emollient and oral antihistamine were not effective. Clinician in transcript diagnosed dermatitis / contact dermatitis and planned topical steroid + stronger emollients and avoidance measures.  
- Working diagnosis and management priorities: Likely occupational irritant contact dermatitis of the palms (working diagnosis) — priorities are avoidance of irritants (consistent glove use), control inflammation (topical steroid per prescription), aggressive emollient therapy, and review for response. Diabetes noted as a risk factor for chronicity/complications.  
- Relevant differential diagnoses from DDx (aligned with transcript): see "Summary of Differential Diagnoses" below. Consider alternative causes if no improvement. Also consider secondary bacterial infection where there is bleeding/cracking.  
- Conflict noted: None between transcript and DDx content.

Management Plan

- Immediate actions and treatments (from transcript): Prescription for a topical steroid to be sent to patient’s pharmacy — medication name/dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript; instruct use of stronger emollients applied to affected hands 3–4 times daily to coat skin.  
- Workplace and avoidance measures: Strong recommendation to wear gloves when cleaning and avoid direct contact with cleaning products where possible.  
- Follow-up and monitoring: Return for review in ~1–2 weeks to assess response; advised to return sooner if spreading, worsening, or new symptoms (e.g., signs of infection).  
- Contingency if no improvement (consistent with DDx reasoning): If symptoms persist or worsen, consider alternative/ additional diagnoses (allergic contact dermatitis, tinea manuum, palmar psoriasis, secondary bacterial infection) and arrange appropriate further evaluation or referral (e.g., dermatology assessment and targeted investigations as indicated).  
- Patient education: Advice given about trigger avoidance, frequent emollient use, and to seek earlier review if worsening or non-response. Prescription will be sent to pharmacy as discussed.

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits): Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral: Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support): Not recorded.  
- CTG registration: Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test): Not recorded.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

- Irritant contact dermatitis (occupational hand dermatitis) — Likelihood: High.  
  - Justification: Strong temporal correlation with job change to housekeeping (~3–4 months), frequent exposure to cleaning agents, admitted inconsistent glove use, palmar distribution with fissuring and pain; clinician impression in transcript supports this.  
- Allergic contact dermatitis — Likelihood: Moderate.  
  - Justification: Occupational exposure to multiple chemicals and new exposures could produce delayed hypersensitivity with itchy, fissured palms; pruritus reported; would require further assessment/patch testing to confirm.  
- Tinea manuum (dermatophyte infection) — Likelihood: Low–Moderate.  
  - Justification: Chronic scaly fissured palmar dermatitis can be fungal; diabetes predisposes to fungal infections. Less supported by history because characteristic fungal features (e.g., typical border, associated foot infection) were not reported; consider if no response to treatment.

Quality checks

- Missing but clinically expected elements: blood pressure and pulse; focused physical examination documentation of the hands (description of lesions, distribution, laterality, photos); height/weight/BMI; formal assessment of glycemic control (recent blood glucose or HbA1c); immunization review; mental health screening; detailed medication doses (Metformin dose not recorded); specific steroid name/dose/route/frequency not documented; any requested investigations (e.g., skin swab/KOH, culture, or patch testing) were not documented.  
- Internal contradictions between transcript and DDx: None identified.  
- Transcript quality comment: Audio transcript clear with minor pauses; history adequate for working diagnosis but lacked formal documented physical examination findings and vital signs.
